title.title: Is federal contract money going to fewer companies?
title.subtitle:
A first look at vendor concentration, FY2008 to FY2025
Suchitra Hole, Shivram Nekkanti, Andy Hannah  |  October 2026
title.notes: Our project asks a simple question: when the federal government buys something, does the money go to many companies or to a few? Here is what we have built so far and what the first look at the data shows.

question.title: The question: many vendors, or a few?
question.goal: Our goal: for every agency, every product and every year, measure whether contract money is spread across many companies or goes to a few.
question.takeaway: When a few companies win most of an agency's money, it has less choice and less price pressure. A high score is not wrongdoing: some things only one firm can build.
question.notes: The government spent about 793 billion dollars on contracts in FY2025. Picture two markets. On the left, five companies split the money evenly. On the right, one company gets 80 percent. Same spending, very different competition. Studies so far mostly look at defense. We measure this for every agency and every product, over 18 years. One caution up front: a concentrated market is not wrongdoing. Only one shipyard builds aircraft carriers. We describe where concentration is and how it changes, not why.

data.title: The data: every federal contract action since FY2008
data.source: Source: USAspending.gov Award Data Archive, contracts, all agencies, release of 2026-09-06.
data.takeaway: Each row says who bought what, from whom, for how much, and whether others could bid. Adding rows up by buyer, product and company shows who wins the money.
data.notes: We downloaded the government's own public archive: one file per fiscal year, 18 files, 88.8 million rows. Each row is one contract action. Here is a real one from September 2025: the Navy paid Lockheed Martin 14.1 billion dollars for fixed-wing aircraft, and it was not competed. Every row has the buyer, the product code, the company, the amount and how it was competed. That is everything we need to measure concentration.

process.title: How we turned 18 zip files into a trusted dataset
process.takeaway: Every number we show traces back to the published files, and the totals agree with the government's own official figures.
process.notes: Before analysing anything we made sure the data is right. Step 1, we checked every file against its checksum and locked it. Step 2, we converted the files to a fast format and proved the copy is exact: the same rows, the same dollars to the cent, the same value in every field. Step 3, we ran 62 quality checks on every row. They found the records that would distort the measure, like a 13.9 billion dollar entry that was reversed in the next year, and a catch-all vendor called Miscellaneous Foreign Awardees. Step 4, we built the analysis tables, and 116 checks confirm they add back to the original data. Our yearly totals match GAO's official numbers within 0.2 percent.

method.title: How we measure concentration
method.takeaway: A score near 10,000 means one company gets almost all the money in that segment. We track the share of dollars that sits in segments above 2,500.
method.notes: We split the spending into segments: one agency buying one product in one year, for example Defense buying fixed-wing aircraft in FY2025. That gives about 365 thousand segments. For each one we compute the HHI, the standard antitrust measure: take each company's percentage share, square it, and add them up. Five equal companies score 2,000. One company with 80 percent scores 6,500. A single company scores 10,000. The merger guidelines call anything above 2,500 highly concentrated, and that is the line we use.

trend.title: Finding 1: concentration has risen to half the money
trend.dip: Part of the FY2024 dip is timing: combat ships and fixed-wing aircraft, two of the largest segments, fell below 2,500 that year and came back in FY2025.
trend.takeaway: Since FY2014, a growing share of federal contract dollars goes to segments where a few companies win most of the money.
trend.notes: This line is the share of each year's contract dollars that sits in highly concentrated segments. In FY2008 it was 43 percent. It held near 40 percent until about FY2014, then climbed to about 50 percent by FY2022, and it is 50 percent in FY2025. The dip in FY2024 is partly timing: two of the biggest defense segments, combat ships and fixed-wing aircraft, dropped below the line that year and came back the next. Big multi-year awards make single years jumpy, so we read the long trend, not one year.

where.title: Finding 2: it is big-ticket products, not small buys
where.takeaway: Concentration sits in expensive things few firms make, like aircraft. Small one-vendor purchases are common, but they are a tiny share of the money.
where.notes: Where is the concentration? Mostly in products. In FY2025, 69 percent of product dollars sat in highly concentrated segments, against 39 percent for services. Research went the other way, from 59 percent down to 35. Here is an example. Defense spending on fixed-wing aircraft went from 22.7 billion dollars in FY2024 to 42 billion in FY2025, and the largest company's share went from 39 percent to 76 percent. Its score more than doubled. And a common worry, lots of tiny sole-source purchases, is not the story: 30 percent of segments have one vendor, but they hold under 2 percent of the money.

next.title: What it means, and what we do next
steps: Define a rising trend that beats chance
Link IT and construction codes across the code changes
Settle the open data decisions with our sponsor
Then group the trends and ask what rising segments have in common
next.notes: Three takeaways. First, the data is solid: the copy is exact, it matches GAO, and product codes mostly carry across the two code changes, so we can follow most segments for all 18 years. Second, a caution: scores jump from year to year. If we call a line rising when it gains 500 points, 38 percent of lines rise, but 28 percent would rise even with their years shuffled, so most of that is noise. Third, next steps: set a rising rule that beats chance, link the IT and construction codes, settle our data decisions with the sponsor, and then group the trends and ask what the rising segments have in common, such as sole-source awards. Thank you.

backup_decisions.title: Backup: the data decisions barely change the picture
backup_decisions.note: V1 applies the decisions as proposed: reversal pairs replaced by their net, the two US Mint rows, MISCELLANEOUS FOREIGN AWARDEES and rows with no vendor ID left out. V8b also leaves out deobligations larger than the award's obligations that year.
backup_decisions.notes: With the proposed data decisions, under 1 percent of segments change concentration band over 18 years, and the trend only moves in FY2008 to FY2010, the years of the large reversed entry and the two US Mint rows. V8b needs flags from a pipeline step that is still running.

backup_codes.title: Backup: product codes mostly carry across the code changes
backup_codes.note: Product code manuals changed on 2011-10-01 and 2020-10-01. Codes that stopped at either change held almost no dollars. New codes took 87% construction and repair in FY2012, and almost all IT in FY2021.
backup_codes.notes: We expected the two code manual changes to cut our 18 years into short eras. They did not: old codes were almost never retired. New codes were added and some spending moved onto them, mostly construction in FY2012 and IT in FY2021. We will link those codes across the changes.

backup_noise.title: Backup: yearly swings are larger than the 500-point cutoff
backup_noise.note: A line is one agency and one product code, FY2012 to FY2020, with at least 6 scored years and $10 million. Shuffling keeps each line's yearly scores and drops their order, so it shows what noise alone produces.
backup_noise.notes: The typical yearly change in HHI is about 360 points in the largest segments and over 1,000 in smaller ones. At a 500-point cutoff, 38 percent of lines rise and 28 percent still rise with their years shuffled. Rising beats chance by about 10 points; falling does not.

backup_vendors.title: Backup: the 10 largest vendors, FY2008 to FY2025
backup_vendors.note: Vendors are parent IDs as recorded at the time of each action. Names are the raw parent name carrying the most dollars, so they lag mergers: the RTX ID shows as United Technologies, and the Leidos ID as SAIC. A dated name list is planned for week 6.
backup_vendors.notes: These are the largest parent companies over 18 years. Names come straight from the records and lag mergers, so we will build a dated name list before naming vendors in results.

backup_features.title: Backup: some fields change coverage over time
backup_features.note: Set-aside and offers fields are blank on many dollars from FY2018, and most of the blank rows are orders under contract vehicles. The order competition field is blank on 75% to 88% of dollars, since it applies only to some orders.
backup_features.notes: Sole-source share is stable at about a third of dollars. Two fields change coverage in FY2018, which matters for explaining concentration later: we will measure them on the parent contract, or only in the years where they are complete.
